title: The hypocrites the Prophet spared
excerpt: Madinah had men the Prophet knew to be hypocrites, one of them named to his face. He refused to kill them. What that shows, and what it leaves open.
body:
Madinah had men who said "we believe" in the mosque and said something else at home. The Qur'an calls them the munafiqun, the hypocrites, and gives them a surah of their own (63) and long passages of al-Tawbah. The Prophet knew who many of them were. He did not kill them.

That fact rarely comes up when people argue about apostasy. I want to set it out with its sources, then say what it proves and what it leaves open.

The man at the head of them

'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul was a chief of the Khazraj. Before the Prophet reached Madinah, some of his people were ready to make him their king. He accepted Islam in public and spent the rest of his life working against it.

On one campaign, after a quarrel between a man of the Muhajirun and a man of the Ansar, he said: "When we return to Madinah, the more honourable will drive out the meaner." The Qur'an quotes the line back at him (63:8). Zayd ibn Arqam reported it; Ibn Ubayy swore he had said nothing, and the Prophet at first took his oath, until the verses came down (al-Bukhari 4900).

'Umar asked permission to strike the neck of "this hypocrite". The Prophet answered: "Leave him, so that people do not say that Muhammad kills his companions" (al-Bukhari 4905; Muslim 2584).

Read that answer slowly. 'Umar calls the man a hypocrite in front of the Prophet, and the Prophet does not correct him. He refuses the killing anyway. The reason he gives is about the community: what it would mean for Muslims to kill a man who stood in their rows, and what the people outside would say.

Words of disbelief, said aloud

Hypocrisy in the Qur'an is mostly hidden. One passage in al-Tawbah describes something else, a disbelief that came out in speech: "They swear by God that they said nothing. But they did say the word of disbelief, and they disbelieved after their Islam" (9:74).

"They disbelieved after their Islam" is about as close as the Qur'an comes to defining riddah in a single phrase. The verse goes on: "If they repent, it is better for them. And if they turn away, God will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter."

The punisher named in the verse is God. The verse offers the men a door, repentance, and gives the Prophet and the believers no order to carry anything out.

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman is remembered as the Companion who knew the names. Muslim reports from him that the Prophet said: "Among my Companions are twelve hypocrites" (Muslim 2779). They went on living in Madinah. The sources I have read record no trial of any of them.

The shirt and the funeral

When Ibn Ubayy died, his son, also called 'Abd Allah and a Muslim in earnest, asked the Prophet for his shirt to shroud his father in. The Prophet gave it, and went to pray over the body.

'Umar took hold of him and asked whether God had not forbidden him to pray over the hypocrites. The Prophet said he had been given a choice, and recited: "Ask forgiveness for them, or do not; even if you ask seventy times, God will not forgive them" (9:80). He prayed. Then 9:84 came down: "Never pray over any of them who dies, and do not stand at his grave" (al-Bukhari 1269).

So the last ruling about Ibn Ubayy concerns a prayer over a dead man. It says what the Prophet may do at a graveside. It says nothing about what should have been done to the man while he lived, because nothing was done.

What the jurists made of it

The classical jurists knew every one of these reports and still held a worldly penalty for open apostasy. The guide on the apostasy penalty sets out their evidence and the modern debate. They reconciled the two in more than one way.

One answer is that a court judges what is shown and proved, and hypocrisy is concealed by definition. Another, which Ibn Taymiyyah works through at length in al-Sarim al-Maslul, is that the Prophet held back for a reason tied to his own time: the very harm he named, of people saying he killed his companions.

I think the first answer is weaker than it looks. The line in 63:8 was heard by a witness, and 9:74 describes a "word of disbelief" that people heard. The Prophet had evidence in front of him, and he left the matter with God.

The second answer is honest about the text. It also concedes the point that matters most to a frightened reader. The Prophet held the power to act, had a named man in front of him, and was offered the sword by 'Umar. He put it aside.

What it does not settle

These reports leave the classical law standing as a position. The jurists had their answers, and there are other reports to weigh, which the rebuttal on apostasy and the classical law takes up.

Two things the story does show. The first community lived for years beside men it knew to be unbelievers, prayed next to them, and buried them. And the Qur'an's own answer to disbelief after belief, in 9:74, was a call to repent and a warning from God.

If you are reading this because you are afraid, the threat you face comes from families, mobs or states, and the rules where you live are in leaving Islam and the law. If you are in danger now, go to where to find support first.

Compelling Evidence has a longer study of the report most often quoted against people who leave, "whoever changes his religion". Allahu a'lam.

The Qur'an quotations are my own renderings of the Arabic, and hadith numbers follow the sunnah.com numbering.

title: The Hudaybiyyah clause on leaving
excerpt: In 628 the Prophet signed a treaty letting any Muslim who went over to Quraysh stay there. What the clause said, and what scholars made of it.
body:
In March 628, the sixth year after the Hijrah, the Prophet camped at al-Hudaybiyyah, on the edge of the sacred precinct of Makkah, with about 1,400 Companions. They had come in pilgrim dress to perform the 'umrah. Quraysh barred the way, and the two sides wrote a treaty instead.

The ten-year truce is the part usually remembered. One clause bears directly on people who leave.

What the clause said

Anas ibn Malik reports the terms in Sahih Muslim. Quraysh stipulated that anyone who came from the Muslims to them would not be returned, and anyone who came from them to the Muslims would be sent back.

The Companions asked: "Messenger of God, shall we write this?" He said: "Yes. Whoever of us goes to them, God has put him far away. And whoever of them comes to us, God will make for him relief and a way out" (Muslim 1784).

So the Prophet put his name to a written term that let any Muslim who chose to cross over to Quraysh stay there, unreturned. Quraysh at that moment was the enemy, the side the Muslims had fought at Badr, Uhud and the Trench. Going over to them meant leaving the religion and the community together, the case the jurists would later treat as the gravest.

He agreed to the clause as written. His comment on it is short, and the verb carries the weight: God has put him far away. It names a loss and leaves the lost man with God.

The cost on the other side

The clause hurt the Muslims, and the sources say so plainly. While the treaty was still being written, Abu Jandal, the son of the Quraysh negotiator Suhayl ibn 'Amr, stumbled into the camp in chains and begged not to be sent back. Suhayl held him to the terms. The Prophet returned him (al-Bukhari 2731).

'Umar was so shaken that he went to the Prophet and then to Abu Bakr asking why they should accept such humiliation in their religion. The Qur'an called the treaty "a clear opening" all the same (48:1).

Soon afterwards the Qur'an ended the clause for one group. Believing women who fled Makkah were not to be sent back to the unbelievers once their faith was tested (60:10).

So the treaty ran one way for men arriving in Madinah and another way for women. For anyone going from Madinah to Makkah, it ran the same way for everyone: they could go.

What scholars made of it

The classical jurists read the clause as a treaty term, agreed under the terms of war and binding because a promise binds. In their view it showed that the ruler could waive pursuit by agreement. It did not, for them, cancel the penalty for apostasy inside Muslim jurisdiction, which they drew from other reports. The case for that penalty, and the case against it, is in the apostasy penalty.

I accept that this is the strongest reading of the treaty as law. I also think the clause tells us something the law books pass over quickly.

The Prophet signed it in a camp full of armed men, at a moment when he could have walked away from the talks. He agreed in writing that a Muslim who left for the enemy would be beyond reach. And the first thing he said about such a man was a sentence about God, with nothing about a sword in it.

The guide what apostasy is in Islamic law explains what riddah means in the law, and why doubts and questions sit outside it.

Why this matters to you

If you are thinking about leaving, you may be carrying a picture of the Prophet as a man who hunted down anyone who turned away. The treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah is a signed document that cuts against that picture. Use it to test the picture, and keep the limits above in mind while you do.

It does not tell you what your family will do, or what the law will do where you live. The rebuttal on the death threat charge deals with threats made in the religion's name, and leaving Islam and the law has the law country by country.

If you would like a reading path that fits where you are right now, there is a short quiz on Compelling Evidence. It takes a few minutes, and your answers stay on your device.

The Qur'an quotations are my own renderings of the Arabic, and hadith numbers follow the sunnah.com numbering.

title: Who may call a Muslim kafir?
excerpt: "You are a kafir now." Doubters hear it from cousins and comment threads. The Prophet warned about that word, and the jurists fenced it in.
body:
Many people who write to sites like this one have heard the sentence. A cousin says it at a wedding. A stranger types it under a video. A parent shouts it through a bedroom door. "You are a kafir now."

The word has a ruling attached to it, and the ruling falls on the person who says it as much as on the person who hears it.

The word that comes back

'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar reports that the Prophet said: "If a man says to his brother, 'O kafir', then it returns to one of the two" (al-Bukhari 6104; Muslim 60). In Muslim's wording: "If it is as he said, so be it. If not, it comes back on him."

Abu Hurayrah reports the same warning (al-Bukhari 6103). Scholars explained it in different ways. Some said the speaker falls into the sin of the word. Others said that if he calls belief itself unbelief, he has said something about Islam that cannot stand. Every explanation I have read treats the word as dangerous to the one who throws it.

Did you split open his heart?

The hardest case in the sources is a battlefield. Usama ibn Zayd, a young commander the Prophet loved, caught up with an enemy fighter who said "la ilaha illa Allah" as Usama raised his sword. Usama killed him anyway, sure the man had said it only to save his life.

When the Prophet heard, he asked: "Did you kill him after he said la ilaha illa Allah?" (al-Bukhari 4269). Usama explained that the man said it out of fear of the weapon. The Prophet answered: "Did you split open his heart, so that you would know whether it said it or not?" Usama said the Prophet repeated it until he wished he had only become a Muslim that day (Muslim 96).

The Qur'an had already given the rule: "Do not say to one who offers you peace, 'You are not a believer'" (4:94).

If a man under the sword was owed the benefit of his words, your cousin owes it to you at a wedding.

The fence the jurists built

The classical law did define apostasy and did attach consequences to it. The guide on what apostasy is in Islamic law sets out the definition. The same law surrounded the judgement with conditions: the person must be an adult of sound mind, must know what he is saying, must say it freely, and must mean it. A question is not a statement of disbelief. Neither is a doubt that frightens the person who has it.

The judgement also belonged to a qualified judge, after an inquiry, and with the accused given time and a hearing. That puts it out of reach of a relative or a commenter.

Al-Ghazali wrote a short book on this, Faysal al-Tafriqa, against the habit of his day of branding other Muslims unbelievers over points of theology. His advice, in Sherman Jackson's translation (On the Boundaries of Theological Tolerance in Islam, Oxford, 2002), is to hold back from the charge wherever there is room to: wrongly leaving a thousand unbelievers alone is a lesser error than wrongly spilling the blood of one Muslim.

If you are the one hearing it

Your doubts do not make you a kafir in the sense the law uses, and the person saying it is neither your judge nor a qualified one. The rebuttal doubt is not hypocrisy deals with the related fear that doubting inside the mosque makes you a hypocrite.

If you have decided that you no longer believe, that is your own statement to make, in your own words and at your own time. No one else needs to make it for you. If the word is being used to threaten you, take it seriously and read where to find support.

If you are the one saying it

Stop. The Prophet asked Usama a question he could not answer, and you cannot answer it either. You do not know what is in your brother's heart, and you do not know how his story ends.

What you can do is listen, answer what you know, and admit what you do not. The guide supporting someone who doubts is written for families in exactly this place.

Best of Islam traces the history of the practice, from the first group that made it a weapon, in the Kharijites and takfir.

The Qur'an quotations are my own renderings of the Arabic, and hadith numbers follow the sunnah.com numbering.

title: Faith that rises and falls
excerpt: The Qur'an says faith increases. The hadith say it wears thin like cloth. A low season is part of the life the texts describe.
body:
Some months the prayers feel full and the Qur'an reads like a letter addressed to you. Other months you stand in the row and feel nothing at all. People in the second kind of month often decide they have already lost their faith, and that the next step is to admit it.

The texts describe faith as something that moves. That changes what a low month means.

The Qur'an on faith that grows

The Qur'an speaks of faith increasing several times. "He is the one who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers, so that they would add faith to their faith" (48:4). The believers are those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned, "and when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith" (8:2).

In the days after Uhud, when the Muslims were told that a great army had gathered against them, "it increased them in faith, and they said: God is enough for us" (3:173). And when a surah came down, some asked which of them it had increased in faith, and the answer came: "As for those who believe, it increased them in faith, and they rejoice" (9:124).

Anything that can increase can also decrease. Al-Bukhari drew that conclusion in the arrangement of his Sahih itself. In the Book of Faith he gave a chapter the heading "The increase of faith and its decrease", and placed under it the report that whoever says la ilaha illa Allah with a barley grain's weight of good in his heart will come out of the Fire (al-Bukhari 44). A barley grain is a small amount. The report counts it.

Faith that wears thin

There is a report I come back to often. The Prophet said: "Faith wears out inside one of you the way a garment wears out, so ask God to renew the faith in your hearts." Al-Hakim records it in al-Mustadrak (no. 5), and al-Albani graded it sahih in al-Silsilah al-Sahihah (no. 1585).

The picture is ordinary cloth. A shirt worn every day thins at the elbows and goes shiny at the collar. It is still the same shirt. You mend it, or you ask for a new one, and the report tells you who to ask.

The Companions knew the feeling. Hanzalah feared he had become a hypocrite because his heart was soft in the Prophet's company and hard at home among his family and fields. The Prophet told him that if they stayed always as they were in his presence, the angels would shake their hands in the streets, and then said: "Hanzalah, an hour and an hour" (Muslim 2750).

A scholarly disagreement worth knowing

I should be honest that Muslim theologians did not all put it the same way. The position linked to Abu Hanifa, and held by many Hanafi and Maturidi scholars after him, is that faith as assent does not grow or shrink: you assent or you do not. What grows and shrinks, on that view, is its light, its certainty and the deeds that come from it.

The two positions agree on the thing that matters here. On both, a believer's inner state goes up and down without that person ceasing to be a believer. They disagree about which word to use for the part that moves.

What a low season is

A low season is a long stretch of the "other hour" Hanzalah described. It can follow a death, an illness, a move, a bad marriage, or nothing you can name. It can also arrive with real questions, and those deserve real answers; the guide how to assess a doubt is a way to sort them.

It helps to keep the two apart. A question about a hadith is a claim to be checked. A flat, grey feeling in prayer is a state, and states move. If you treat the state as though it were an argument, you can talk yourself into a conclusion the evidence never gave you.

If you have stopped praying and the guilt is crushing you, read the guilt of not praying. For a longer account of one scholar's crisis and how he came through it, al-Ghazali's is in doubt and the inner life.

Asking for the new garment

The report gives an instruction with the diagnosis: ask God to renew it. That is a small prayer, and you can say it on a day when you feel nothing, in your own language, in a sentence.

Some people find that a fixed small act helps more than a large resolution: 2 rak'ahs at night, a page of the Qur'an with a translation, one honest conversation. The Prophet said the deeds God loves most are the ones done steadily, even when they are small (al-Bukhari 6464).

If you are not sure where to start reading, try a short quiz on Compelling Evidence. It suggests a reading path from a few questions about where you are.

title: They ask you: questions in the Qur'an
excerpt: "They ask you" opens one answer after another in the Qur'an. The book was revealed into a room of people asking questions, and it kept answering.
body:
Open the Qur'an at the second surah and read to the end of it. You will find the words "they ask you" (yas'alunaka) again and again, each time followed by an answer.

They asked about the new moons (2:189). About what to spend, and on whom (2:215). About fighting in the sacred month (2:217), wine and gambling (2:219), the orphans in their care (2:220), and menstruation (2:222). Later surahs carry on: the spoils of war (8:1), the spirit (17:85), Dhu al-Qarnayn (18:83), the mountains on the Last Day (20:105), and over and over, the Hour (7:187; 79:42).

The people asking were the first Muslims, and some of the time they were the Prophet's opponents. The Qur'an put their questions into its own text and answered them there.

Answers that admit something

Some of those answers concede a point. On wine and gambling the Qur'an says: "In them is great sin, and some benefit for people, and their sin is greater than their benefit" (2:219). The verse grants the benefit first and then weighs it.

On the spirit it says: "Say: the spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little" (17:85). The answer is an honest limit. Al-Faruqi made that limit a rule of knowledge: stay open to new evidence and end with Allahu a'lam, because the truth is bigger than any one person can master.

A Bedouin once asked the Prophet when the Hour would come. He answered with a question: "What have you prepared for it?" The man said he had prepared little, except that he loved God and His Messenger, and the Prophet told him: "You will be with those you love" (al-Bukhari 6171).

The questions the Qur'an discouraged

There is one verse people quote to shut questions down: "O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if they were made plain to you, would trouble you" (5:101).

Read it with its setting. It came while the law was still being revealed, when a question could produce a new obligation. The Prophet explained the danger himself: the gravest wrong a Muslim can do to the Muslims is to ask about something that was not forbidden, so that it becomes forbidden because he asked (al-Bukhari 7289; Muslim 2358).

The verse is about piling up rules. A person trying to find out whether the religion is true is asking something else, and the verse leaves that question alone.

The cure for not knowing

A group of travellers once had a man among them with a head wound. He became ritually impure in the night and asked whether he could pray with dry ablution. They told him he had to wash. He washed and died.

When the Prophet heard, he was angry: "They killed him, may God kill them. Why did they not ask when they did not know? The cure for not knowing is to ask" (Abu Dawud 336). Al-Albani graded the report hasan, with a reservation about one phrase at its end.

The Qur'an gives the same instruction in general terms: "Ask the people of knowledge if you do not know" (16:43).

The best-known hadith in the religion is itself a conversation of questions. A stranger in white sits knee to knee with the Prophet and asks what Islam is, what faith is, what doing good is, and when the Hour will come. After he leaves, the Prophet says: "That was Jibril. He came to teach you your religion" (Muslim 8). The religion was taught by someone asking.

What this means if you have questions

Your questions have a place in this tradition, at its centre. The first community asked, sometimes awkwardly, and the answers came down in the book they recited in prayer.

Two cautions from the same sources. Ask people who know, which is the point of 16:43, and which the people who killed the wounded man forgot. And expect some answers to end with a limit, the way 17:85 does. A limit is an answer too.

If your question is whether you can believe without being sure, start with belief without knowing. If it is about a verse that troubles you, the guide reading the Qur'an in context shows how to read one in its setting, and how to assess a doubt gives a method for any question at all.

And if you have more questions than you know what to do with, a short quiz on Compelling Evidence will suggest a place to begin.

The Qur'an quotations are my own renderings of the Arabic, and hadith numbers follow the sunnah.com numbering.

title: Rajab and the four sacred months
excerpt: Rajab 1448 begins on 10 December 2026. The verse about fighting in Rajab is also a verse about leaving Islam. What it says, read whole.
body:
Rajab 1448 begins today, Thursday 10 December 2026, by the Umm al-Qura calendar used in Saudi Arabia. Where the month is fixed by sighting the new moon, it may begin a day later.

Rajab is one of the four sacred months. The Qur'an names their number, and one verse about this month is also one of the verses the law of apostasy is built on.

Four months out of twelve

"The number of months with God is twelve months in the book of God, from the day He created the heavens and the earth. Four of them are sacred. That is the right religion, so do not wrong yourselves in them" (9:36).

The Prophet named the four in his sermon at the farewell pilgrimage: "The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: three in a row, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram, and the Rajab of Mudar, which comes between Jumada and Sha'ban" (al-Bukhari 4662; Muslim 1679).

The Arabs before Islam already kept these months as a truce, and the tribe of Mudar kept Rajab more strictly than others, which is why the sermon names it after them. The Qur'an kept the truce and gave it a reason that reaches past war: do not wrong yourselves in them. Al-Tabari reports from Ibn 'Abbas that the wrong is forbidden in every month, and these four were singled out to make it graver.

What the month does not have

Rajab has gathered popular customs over the centuries, special prayers and fasts said to carry a set reward. Ibn Hajar al-'Asqalani examined the reports behind them in a short book, Tabyin al-'Ajab bima warada fi Fadl Rajab, and judged the reports of special virtues for this month weak or invented. The sacredness of the month comes from 9:36 and the farewell sermon. The rest came later.

I mention it because a person in doubt often meets the religion through its customs first. If a custom has no sound basis, that is a finding about the custom. It tells you nothing yet about the Qur'an.

The raid at Nakhlah

In the second year after the Hijrah, the Prophet sent 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh with a small party to Nakhlah, between Makkah and al-Ta'if, to watch Quraysh. On what may have been the last day of Rajab they attacked a Quraysh caravan, killed a man named 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami, and took two prisoners. Ibn Ishaq tells the story, in Ibn Hisham's Sirah.

Quraysh made the most of it: Muhammad's men had shed blood in the sacred month. The Prophet would not accept the spoils at first. Then the verse came down that begins "They ask you about the sacred month":

"Say: fighting in it is grave. But barring people from the way of God, disbelief in Him and in the Sacred Mosque, and driving its people out of it, are graver with God. And persecution is graver than killing. They will not stop fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they can. And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, their deeds have come to nothing in this world and the Hereafter. Those are the people of the Fire; they will be in it forever" (2:217).

Reading the verse whole

Look at the order. The verse first admits that the Muslim party did something grave. Then it names a graver wrong, which is persecution: Quraysh fighting the believers "until they turn you back from your religion". Apostasy enters the verse as something Quraysh were trying to force on Muslims by war.

Then comes the sentence about the person who turns back. Its consequence has two conditions, that he turns back and that he dies a disbeliever, and the loss it names is the loss of his deeds. It sets no penalty for anyone to carry out. The classical penalty rests on hadith, a point the guide what apostasy is in Islamic law makes with the texts, and the apostasy penalty examines those hadith.

The second condition matters. "And dies while he is a disbeliever" leaves the door open for as long as the person is alive. Scholars disagreed about whether the deeds of someone who leaves and comes back are restored, and the guide coming back after leaving sets that disagreement out. The verse itself sets the line at death.

A month for doing less harm

So the sacred month asks for less harm, and asks it of believers first: "do not wrong yourselves in them." If someone in your family is doubting or has left, this month is a good time to stop the argument at the dinner table and treat them as the verse treats every person, as someone whose last word has not been written yet.

And if you are the one doubting, the month asks nothing of you that it does not ask of everyone. Read, and take your time. If fear is doing the thinking for you, read the fear itself.

Best of Islam has more on how Islam treated the rites it inherited from pre-Islamic Arabia, the sacred months among them, in Islamic rites before Islam.

The Qur'an quotations are my own renderings of the Arabic, and hadith numbers follow the sunnah.com numbering.

title: When someone who left Islam dies
excerpt: A brother, a parent or a friend left Islam and has now died. What the rulings say about the funeral, and what they leave open to love.
focus_keyword: funeral of someone who left Islam
body:
This post is for a Muslim whose brother, mother, child or friend left Islam and has now died. It is also for anyone who has left and lies awake wondering what their family will do when that day comes.

The rulings are real, and I will state them plainly. They are narrower than the grief around them, and the texts leave a great deal of room for love.

What the rulings say

The funeral prayer, salat al-janazah, is a prayer of the Muslims for a Muslim. The classical scholars held that it is not offered over someone who died outside Islam. They took this from 9:84, revealed about the hypocrites of Madinah, and from 9:113: "It is not for the Prophet and the believers to ask forgiveness for the idolaters, even if they are near of kin, after it has become clear to them that they are people of the Fire."

The second verse has a story behind it. When the Prophet's uncle Abu Talib was dying, the Prophet sat with him and pleaded with him to say la ilaha illa Allah. Abu Talib died on the religion of his fathers. The Prophet said: "I will keep asking forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden." Then 9:113 came down (al-Bukhari 1360).

Read what the story shows about the Prophet. The man who died outside Islam was the uncle who raised him and shielded him for years in Makkah, and the Prophet's first reaction was to keep praying for him.

What the rulings leave open

Almost everything else.

When Abu Talib died, 'Ali came to the Prophet and said: "Your uncle, the old man who went astray, has died." The Prophet told him: "Go and bury your father." 'Ali did, and the Prophet told him to wash afterwards (Abu Dawud 3214; al-Albani graded it sahih). So the Prophet sent his own cousin to bury a father who died outside the religion.

The Prophet asked God's permission to seek forgiveness for his mother, Aminah, and was refused. He asked permission to visit her grave, and it was granted. Abu Hurayrah says he went to the grave, wept, and made those around him weep, and then said: "Visit the graves, for they remind you of death" (Muslim 976).

So the sources allow you to grieve, to weep at the grave, to bury, to sit with the family, to speak well of the person, and to keep their memory. The Qur'an tells the believers to "speak to people kindly" (2:83), and it makes no exception for the dead.

Who knows how it ended

There is also a limit on what any of us can say about the person. The Prophet said: "Deeds are judged by their endings" (al-Bukhari 6607). You did not see the last hour of their life from the inside. Neither did anyone else.

The funeral rulings follow what was outwardly known about the person, because a community has to decide what to do at a graveside. The person's standing before God belongs to God alone, who "does not wrong anyone by the weight of an atom" (4:40). Sunni creed has long held back from declaring that any named individual is in the Fire, and I think that restraint applies with special force to someone you loved and cannot ask.

When the law gets involved

In some countries the dispute over a body is a legal one. Where religion is recorded by the state, a person who left may still be registered as a Muslim, and the family can end up in court over who buries them and how. Malaysia is one example among several. In 2005 the High Court declined to hear the widow of the mountaineer M. Moorthy after the Syariah Court had declared him a convert to Islam, and he was buried as a Muslim against her wishes.

If this could happen to you, write down your wishes, tell someone you trust, and find out how registration works where you live. religion by registration explains how the state's record and a person's belief come apart, and leaving Islam and the law gives the law by region.

If you are the one grieving

Grief and theology arrive tangled together. You may feel guilt for not having argued more, or anger at the person, or at God, or at the people around you who speak about your loss as a verdict. The doubt doubts after a death is written for that tangle.

If you are a family member trying to hold the others together, the guide supporting someone who doubts was written for the living, and much of it still applies. And if grief has become too heavy to carry alone, where to find support lists places that can help.

Compelling Evidence has a longer study of the verse that governs every choice in this post, no compulsion in religion. Allahu a'lam.

The Qur'an quotations are my own renderings of the Arabic, and hadith numbers follow the sunnah.com numbering.

title: Taking stock at the year's end
excerpt: The Qur'an asks every soul to look at what it has sent ahead. A year-end reckoning for a doubter: what you asked, what you found, what you did.
body:
The calendar most of us live by turns over this week. The Muslim year turned earlier, in June, when 1448 began. Either date will do for what follows.

"O you who believe, be mindful of God, and let every soul look at what it has sent ahead for tomorrow" (59:18). The scholars called this looking muhasabah, taking account of oneself. It is an old practice, and it suits a person in doubt better than they might expect.

A saying and its grading

A report often quoted on this subject says: "The shrewd one is he who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death, and the helpless one is he who follows his desires and then hopes for things from God." Al-Tirmidhi records it (no. 2459). Al-Albani graded its chain weak, so I would not build on it as a saying of the Prophet.

Right after it, al-Tirmidhi quotes 'Umar: "Take account of yourselves before you are taken to account." That is a saying of 'Umar, and it is reported as his. The idea needs no weak chain. The Qur'an already puts the account in your own hands: "Read your book. Your own self is enough today to take account of you" (17:14).

Why a doubter needs this more

Doubt has a way of turning a year into fog. You remember being upset and reading a lot. You may not remember what you actually read, which arguments moved you, and which ones you never checked.

A reckoning puts dates and names back into the fog. It is also fair to both sides of the question. If Islam is true, an honest account of your year helps you. If you are leaving, an honest account helps you leave for reasons you can state.

A way to do it

Take a sheet of paper, or a private file, and write four lists.

The questions you started the year with. Write them as sentences, the way you would ask them out loud.

What you read or heard on each one, with the source. A video counts, and so does a cousin. Next to each, mark whether you checked it against anything.

Which questions are claims and which are feelings. "The hadith were written down two centuries later" is a claim, and it can be checked; start with the two-centuries gap. "I feel nothing when I pray" is a state, and states move. The guide how to assess a doubt is built around this distinction.

What you did. Prayers kept or dropped, conversations had or avoided, kindnesses and the other kind. This list is the one 59:18 is asking for, and 99:7-8 says nothing on it is too small to count, "whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it."

What to do with the lists

Read the first list again. Some questions will have answers now; cross them off and note where the answer came from. Some will have answers you do not like. Leave those on the list, honestly marked.

Look hard at the second list. If every source on it pulls in one direction, from one corner of the internet, you have not yet heard the case. The doubt the websites is about that pattern.

Pick one thing from the fourth list to carry into the new year. One. The Prophet said the deeds God loves most are the ones done steadily, even if small (al-Bukhari 6464; Muslim 783).

If the account frightens you

Some people sit down to do this and find a year they are ashamed of. The Qur'an does not ask you to look so that you can despair: "Say: O My servants who have wronged themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God" (39:53).

If you have left and are thinking of coming back, the doubt can I come back? and the guide coming back after leaving answer the question directly. If you are staying and still unsure, that is a place many believers have stood, and the year ahead has room for it.

For a reading path to start the new year with, try a short quiz on Compelling Evidence. It asks a few questions and points you somewhere to begin.

The Qur'an quotations are my own renderings of the Arabic, and hadith numbers follow the sunnah.com numbering.
